binders: A dimension m; vector field q; flux; proposed derivative fields qt and fluxx; a fixed time t.
hypotheses: The integral conservation law holds for every interval and time.
For every x, qt(x) is the time derivative of q(x,.) at t and fluxx(x) is the space derivative of flux(q(.,t)) at x.
qt and fluxx are interval-integrable on every real interval.
For every interval, time differentiation may be interchanged with integrating q at t, yielding the integral of qt.
The residual x -> qt(x)+fluxx(x) is continuous.
conclusions: For every x, q satisfies the pointwise differential conservation residual q_t+(flux(q))_x=0 at (x,t).
mathematical_definitions: The integral law uses the oriented interval integral and boundary term flux(q(a,t))-flux(q(b,t)).
The local law existentially witnesses the time derivative and spatial flux derivative and sets their sum to zero.
translation.proposition_plain_english: At a fixed time, an integral conservation law implies the pointwise differential conservation equation, provided explicit derivative fields exist, are integrable on every interval, differentiation under every interval integral is valid, and their sum is continuous.

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: The conclusion is conditional on numerous strong global hypotheses, including interchange of differentiation and integration for every pair of real endpoints and continuity of the residual.
The dimension m may be zero.
The theorem is at one fixed time and does not itself provide the derivative fields, their integrability, or the interchange theorem.
The integral convention is oriented and uses the boundary term flux at the left endpoint minus flux at the right endpoint.
